---
title: "Reading R's own object header"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Every R object lives in memory behind a fixed-size C header, the `SEXPREC`: a word of
bitfields, three pointers and, for a vector, its length. A fixed-size record is exactly what
`bin_layout()` describes, so the header makes a small worked example of a layout over bytes
that zubin did not write: native byte order, a bitfield word, pointers, and a body at a known
offset.

This is a way to look, not a way to program. The structure is private to R (it is in R's
`Defn.h`, not in its API), it changes between R versions, and nothing here belongs in a
package. To inspect an object in earnest use `lobstr::sxp()`, or `.Internal(inspect(x))` at
the console; the last section says how each reads the header.
The page assumes a 64-bit build of R 4.x, where the header is 48 bytes.

## Getting the bytes

zubin reads raw vectors, and no R function hands over an object's own memory, so the page
compiles a three-line C function that copies the first `n` bytes of the header into one:

```{r peek}
stopifnot(.Machine$sizeof.pointer == 8)
library(zubin)

src <- tempfile(fileext = ".c")
writeLines(c(
  "#include <string.h>",
  "#include <Rinternals.h>",
  "SEXP peek(SEXP x, SEXP n) {",
  "  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(RAWSXP, Rf_asInteger(n)));",
  "  memcpy(RAW(out), (const void *) x, (size_t) XLENGTH(out));",
  "  UNPROTECT(1);",
  "  return out;",
  "}"
), src)
system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "R"), c("CMD", "SHLIB", shQuote(src)), stdout = FALSE)
dll <- dyn.load(sub("\\.c$", .Platform$dynlib.ext, src))
peek <- function(x, n = 48L) .Call(dll$peek, x, n)
```

`peek()` copies as many bytes as it is asked for, and nothing checks them against the object:
the caller asks for no more than the object holds. An integer vector of three elements holds
48 bytes of header and 12 of data.

```{r dump}
x <- c(10L, 20L, 30L)
b <- peek(x, 60L)
bin_hexdump(b)
```

## The layout

On a 64-bit build the header is:

| Offset | Field | C type |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `sxpinfo` | 64 bits of bitfields |
| 8 | `attrib` | `SEXP`, the attribute pairlist |
| 16 | `gengc_next_node` | `SEXP`, the garbage collector's list |
| 24 | `gengc_prev_node` | `SEXP` |
| 32 | `length` | `R_xlen_t`, vectors only |
| 40 | `truelength` | `R_xlen_t`, vectors only |
| 48 | the data | what `INTEGER(x)`, `REAL(x)` and the rest point to |

This is memory of the running process, so the byte order is the host's: `=`, never a guess
at little-endian. `sxpinfo` is two `u32` because a `u64` that holds bitfields can pass 2^53,
past what a double holds exactly; the pointers are user-space addresses, far below 2^53, and
read as `b8` to be printed in hexadecimal. `next` is a reserved word in R, so the pointer
fields take other names.

```{r layout}
header <- bin_layout(
  "= info:u32[2] attrib:b8 gc_next:b8 gc_prev:b8 length:i64 truelength:i64"
)
header
```

```{r unpack}
h <- bin_unpack(b, header)
h[c("length", "truelength")]
bin_decode(b, "i32", offset = 48, n = h$length, endian = "native")
```

## The bitfields

zubin has no bitfield type: a field is whole bytes. The bits come out with arithmetic on the
two words. GCC and Clang allocate bitfields from the least significant bit on the targets R
runs on, which gives, in R 4.x:

| Word | Bits | Field |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0--4 | `type`, the `SEXPTYPE` (13 is `INTSXP`) |
| 1 | 5, 6, 7 | `scalar`, `obj` (has a class), `alt` (ALTREP) |
| 1 | 8--23 | `gp`, general-purpose bits |
| 1 | 24--27 | `mark`, `debug`, `trace`, `spare` |
| 1 | 28, 29--31 | `gcgen`, `gccls` (the collector's generation and size class) |
| 2 | 0--15 | `named`, the reference count |
| 2 | 16--31 | `extra` |

```{r sxpinfo}
bits <- function(v, from, width) (v %/% 2^from) %% 2^width

sxpinfo <- function(h) {
  w1 <- h$info.1
  w2 <- h$info.2
  data.frame(
    type = bits(w1, 0, 5), scalar = bits(w1, 5, 1), obj = bits(w1, 6, 1),
    alt = bits(w1, 7, 1), gp = bits(w1, 8, 16), gcgen = bits(w1, 28, 1),
    gccls = bits(w1, 29, 3), named = bits(w2, 0, 16)
  )
}

address <- function(p) paste0("0x", sub("^0+", "", paste(rev(as.character(p)), collapse = "")))

sxpinfo(h)
```

## What the header shows

A second binding to the same vector raises its reference count, and copies nothing:

```{r refcount}
refs <- function(x) sxpinfo(bin_unpack(peek(x), header))$named
before <- refs(x)
y <- x
c(before = before, after = refs(x))
```

Without attributes, `attrib` points to `NULL`, which is one object of its own, so every bare
object points to the same address. An attribute makes it a pairlist of its own:

```{r attrib}
attrib <- function(x) address(bin_unpack(peek(x), header)$attrib[[1]])
z <- structure(c(1, 2), units = "cm")
c(double = attrib(c(1, 2)), string = attrib("a"), with_attr = attrib(z))
```

`1:3` is an ALTREP object, a compact sequence that stores its start and end, not its
elements: `alt` is set, and the 16 bytes at offset 32 hold ALTREP's own pointers, not a
length.

```{r altrep}
sxpinfo(bin_unpack(peek(1:3), header))[c("type", "alt")]
```

A class sets `obj`:

```{r obj}
sxpinfo(bin_unpack(peek(factor("a")), header))[c("type", "obj")]
```

The same fields, as R prints them; the `ATTRIB` address is the one `attrib()` read above:

```{r inspect}
.Internal(inspect(z))
```

## How the real tools read the header

`peek()` is one of three ways to see these fields, and the only one that can break without
warning.

- **`.Internal(inspect(x))` is part of R.** It is compiled from R's own sources against the
  private `Defn.h`, in the same build as the structure it prints, so it can read every bit
  and never falls out of step with the layout. Its output format is not promised, and
  `.Internal()` is for R's own code: use it at the console, never in a package.
- **`lobstr::sxp()` reads nothing directly.** It asks R through the API: `TYPEOF()`,
  `ALTREP()`, `Rf_isObject()`, `XLENGTH()`, `ANY_ATTRIB()` and `R_mapAttrib()`, and for the
  reference count `NO_REFERENCES()` and `MAYBE_SHARED()`. The address it prints is the
  pointer's value, never dereferenced. It shows less as a result: references as 0, 1 or 2+,
  and no `gp` bits, collector state or `truelength`. Where R 4.5 replaced an accessor,
  lobstr follows behind `#if R_VERSION` guards.
- **`peek()` and a layout** copy the memory and decode it against a description of a
  private structure. That is how it shows the exact reference count and the collector's
  size class, which the API does not expose; it is also why a change to the structure in a
  later R makes it print wrong numbers rather than fail.

Code that runs anywhere but your own console belongs with the second.
